title: The temple of his body (John 2:13–25)
hookLine: destroy this temple and in three days I'll raise it
last: THE BEST WAS KEPT TILL LAST.

lines: LUKE PUTS IT LAST; JOHN PUTS IT FIRST.
cards: Jesus in the temple, driving out the traders: Luke tells that scene at the end, in the last week. John puts it here, in chapter two, right at the start. Christians explain that in different ways.
Some think it happened twice, once early and once late. Others think John placed it at the start on purpose, so it would frame the whole story.
Either way, it's Passover, the city is full, and Jesus walks into the temple and finds it full of cattle, sheep, doves, and the tables of money changers.

teach.h: A WHIP OF CORDS, TABLES OVERTURNED.
teach.b: Some readers point out that the traders were serving pilgrims, who needed animals for the offerings. But Jesus makes a whip of small cords, drives out the sheep and oxen, pours out the coins, and turns over the tables.
To the dove sellers he says: "Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise." My Father's house. The leaders ask him for a sign: what gives you the right?
And he answers with a riddle: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." They hear it literally, and who wouldn't?
"Forty and six years was this temple in building, and wilt thou rear it up in three days?"
Then John tells us what the listeners missed: "But he spake of the temple of his body." For Israel, the temple was the place of God's presence among the people.

John reads Jesus's riddle this way: that place is now a person, Jesus's own body. And even the disciples didn't get it at the time. Only after he was raised from the dead did they remember he'd said this, and believe.
Christians later carried the idea one step further.

teach.h: BUT HE SPAKE OF THE TEMPLE OF HIS BODY.
teach.b: Paul reminds the church in Corinth that "your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you." So for Paul the ordinary body, the one that gets tired and hungry and sore, is holy ground.

how: Some lectionaries set John's account of the temple in Lent, and Paul's words that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit shape Christian teaching about health, rest and the care of the body.

o: show me where it is written.
destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.

games.why: "destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." they hear a building. John says he spoke of the temple of his body.

practice: Move your attention slowly up from your feet, legs, back, shoulders, hands, face, and notice where you're tired, tense or sore, without judging it.
Then choose one kind thing for your body today, a glass of water, a walk, an early night, not to fix how you look but to honor where you live. If you pray, you can give thanks for your body.

wordCard.voice: Naos, the Greek word for the sanctuary, the inner house of God: what John says Jesus meant by destroy this temple, his own body, which would be raised in three days.

orig.note: Greek: the sanctuary, the inner house of God. John uses it for 'this temple' in 2:19, not the word for the whole temple complex.

carryVoice: Your line: a temple of flesh. The place of God's presence, John says, became a person. Day five hundred ninety-eight, done.
